title: The man born blind. Part 1
scripture_text: ‘’As he went along, he saw a man blind from birth. His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” “Neither this man nor his parents sinned,”said Jesus, “but this happened so that the works of God might be displayed in him. As long as it is day, we must do the works of him who sent me. Night is coming, when no one can work. While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” After saying this, he spit on the ground, made some mud with the saliva, and put it on the man’s eyes. “Go,” he told him, “wash in the Pool of Siloam” (this word means “Sent”). So the man went and washed, and came home seeing.’’
devotional:
This is a passage in the word of God that is both demanding and challenging. It is demanding and challenging because it makes us asks more questions than it answers,

Questions like: -

Is some suffering the result of sin, while other suffering isn’t?

If so, then how can we tell if suffering is the result of sin?

Do we need to know if suffering is the consequence of sin?

Would such knowledge make us judgmental of others?

If suffering is not the direct consequence of a person’s sin does that mean that the suffering has been given to display the work of God in his life?

These are some of the questions we need to grapple with as we approach this passage.

The context of the passage.

This blind man was healed during the feast of Tabernacles.

John intends us to connect this healing with the previous chapter, as the references to Jesus as the light of the world indicate (8:12; 9:5). The connection between the healing of the blind man and the Feast of Tabernacles is seen in two ways: -

1. During the festival, large candelabra were lit in the temple courts. Because of the temple's elevated location, the light was visible throughout the city. "The light symbolized the revelation and truth of the Jewish faith" (Gower, 358-359).

At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus declared himself to be ‘the light of the world’ (8:12), a claim that he reiterates in 9:5.

2. At the festival, priests poured water from the Pool of Siloam onto the temple steps "so that it would flow down and out through the Temple to the world outside, and so indicate the way that the Jewish faith would satisfy the world" (Gower, 358). The Pool of Siloam is the place where Jesus will tell the blind man to wash the mud from his eyes. Just as a miraculous feeding of thousands with bread and fish illustrates that Jesus is the bread of life (6:1-14, 35-65); so now he illustrates that he is the light of the world by giving sight to a man in darkness.
prayer: Father I confess that sometimes we want to hold onto and protect our blindness.
